name: YoungArts National Competition
summary: Prestigious national arts competition for US artists ages 15–18 in 10 disciplines including visual art, writing, dance, film, and music, with cash prizes from $250 to $10,000.
subject: Art
description: All applicants are reviewed by panels of esteemed artists in a rigorous multi-round adjudication. Winners with Distinction are invited to an all-expenses-paid National YoungArts Week in Miami, featuring workshops and mentorship from leading professional artists. High school senior winners are eligible to be nominated as U.S. Presidential Scholars in the Arts. The 2027 application cycle closes October 6, 2026.
eligibility: US citizens or permanent residents ages 15–18 or in grades 10–12 as of December 1 of competition year
cost: $35 application fee per discipline; fee waivers available via a simple request letter
deadline: Application typically opens July and closes early October; 2027 cycle closes October 6, 2026

name: Adroit Prizes for Poetry & Prose
summary: Annual literary prizes awarded to outstanding high school and undergraduate writers in poetry and prose, with $200 cash and publication in The Adroit Journal.
subject: Humanities
description: Two prizes are awarded annually—one for poetry (up to 5 poems, max 10 pages) and one for prose (up to 3 works, combined 3,500-word limit). Winners and runners-up are considered for publication in The Adroit Journal, a highly regarded literary magazine. The 2026 prizes were judged by Leila Chatti (poetry) and Karissa Chen (prose). Submissions open April 1–May 1 annually; there is a $15 submission fee with fee assistance available.
eligibility: All secondary and undergraduate students worldwide, including international students
cost: $15 submission fee per entry; fee assistance available through the journal
deadline: Submissions open April 1 and close May 1 each year (2026 extended to May 12)

name: John Locke Institute Global Essay Prize
summary: Prestigious international argumentative essay competition for students under 19, covering 10 humanities/social science categories, with scholarships up to $10,000.
subject: Humanities
description: Students choose one of 10 subject categories—including Philosophy, Politics, Economics, History, Psychology, Law, and International Relations—and write a rigorous argumentative essay of up to 2,000 words in response to a set question. Prizes are awarded as scholarships toward John Locke Institute programs: $5,000 (1st), $2,000 (2nd), $1,000 (3rd) per category, plus a $10,000 Grand Prize for the best essay overall. Shortlisted finalists are invited to an academic conference and awards dinner in London in October. The competition draws tens of thousands of entries from more than 150 countries and is free to enter.
eligibility: Students of any age under 19 as of May 31 of competition year; open worldwide
cost: Free to enter; optional London gala attendance is not free
deadline: Regular submission deadline is May 31 annually; awards dinner October 3, 2026

name: VFW Voice of Democracy Scholarship Program
summary: Annual audio-essay competition for US high school students (grades 9–12) on a patriotic theme, with over $2.1 million in total scholarships and a $35,000 national grand prize.
subject: Humanities
description: Students record a 3–5 minute audio essay on a patriotic theme set by the VFW Commander-in-Chief and submit it with a typed transcript to a local VFW post by October 31. Winners advance through post, district, and state levels before competing nationally. The national first-place winner receives a $35,000 scholarship paid to an American college or vocational school; other national scholarships range from $1,000 to $15,000. Nearly 40,000 students participate annually.
eligibility: US citizen students in grades 9–12; entry must be submitted to a local sponsoring VFW post
cost: Free to enter; submitted through local VFW posts
deadline: Student entry deadline is October 31 each year

name: Princeton University Ten-Minute Play Contest
org: Lewis Center for the Arts, Princeton University
summary: Highly selective annual playwriting competition exclusively for 11th-grade students worldwide, with cash prizes up to $500 and judging by Princeton theater faculty.
subject: Humanities
description: High school juniors (11th graders in the US or international equivalent) submit one original, unpublished play of up to 10 pages (1 page = 1 minute of stage time). The contest is capped at 250 entries and often closes before the deadline. Prizes are $500 (1st), $250 (2nd), and $100 (3rd), with finalists and honorable mentions also recognized. Collaborative submissions are allowed if all writers are eligible juniors. Winners are published on the contest page after June 22, 2026.
eligibility: Students in 11th grade (US or international equivalent); one play per student; must be written in English
cost: Free to enter
deadline: Typically opens in spring and closes when 250 entries are received or by a set spring deadline; winners announced after June 22

name: Doodle for Google
summary: Annual K–12 art competition inviting US students to reimagine the Google logo around a creative theme, with the national winner's doodle featured on Google.com and a $30,000+ college scholarship.
subject: Art
description: Each year, Google challenges K–12 students to create an original doodle illustrating a set theme using any visual art medium—drawing, painting, sculpture (photographed), collage, or digital illustration. Entries are judged on artistic skill, creativity, and how effectively the theme is communicated. Five national finalists are selected and their doodles appear on Google's homepage; public voting then determines the National Winner. The 2025–2026 theme was 'My superpower is…' with a judging panel including NBA player Giannis Antetokounmpo; a national winner was announced in June 2026.
eligibility: K–12 students enrolled in US schools; one entry per student; submitted by a parent, teacher, or school program
cost: Free to enter; submitted by parents, teachers, or school programs on behalf of students
deadline: 2025–2026 cycle deadline was December 17, 2025; winners announced June 2026

name: iCivics Youth Fellowship
summary: A paid, 10-month national civic leadership fellowship for 34 selected U.S. high school students (grades 9–12) that builds leadership, communications, and civic education skills.
subject: Leadership
description: Now in its seventh year, the fellowship selects 34 students from across the country through a competitive process. Fellows engage in virtual workshops, expert lectures, collaborative projects, and an in-person symposium in Washington, D.C. The yearlong program runs August through May, focusing on youth perspectives on civic education, dialogue across differences, and strengthening democracy. Alumni can continue as civics ambassadors and mentors to future cohorts.
eligibility: U.S. high school students grades 9–12; requires educator/mentor recommendation; open to all backgrounds
cost: Paid fellowship — fellows receive a stipend; travel covered for in-person events
deadline: Applications open each spring; fellows notified in July; fellowship begins in August

name: UNICEF USA National Youth Council
summary: A fully funded, year-long structured volunteer leadership role for youth ages 14–24 to advance child rights through national advocacy, campaigns, and youth-led policy engagement.
subject: Leadership
description: Council members work closely with UNICEF USA staff to elevate youth voices, lead issue-specific campaigns, support the club and volunteer network, and advocate for policy change. The role requires 3–5 hours per week, weekly virtual meetings, and participation in a mandatory in-person fall retreat (travel fully covered). Members receive a $1,000 stipend and gain practical skills in volunteer organizing, civic engagement, communications, and advocacy. Applications for 2026–2027 were open as of early 2026.
eligibility: Ages 14–24; must reside in the U.S. during term; interest in advocacy and organizing; reliable internet access required
cost: Fully funded; $1,000 stipend provided; travel and lodging covered for in-person retreat
deadline: Applications for 2026–2027 were open in early 2026; check unicefusa.org for current cycle

name: Student Conservation Association – National Conservation Crews
summary: A summer volunteer program where crews of 6–10 high school students live and work in U.S. national parks, forests, and wildlife refuges on multi-week conservation service projects.
subject: Biology
description: High school participants ages 15–19 join crews that build trails, restore habitats, and complete essential conservation projects on public lands across the country. Crews live on-site in tents, cook their own meals, and are supervised by experienced adult crew leaders. Programs typically run 15–35 days from June through August, building environmental awareness, social responsibility, leadership, and teamwork skills. The SCA is the largest provider of hands-on conservation programs for youth in the U.S.
eligibility: High school students ages 15–19; no prior wilderness experience required; U.S. residents
cost: Free to participants; all program costs covered
deadline: Applications open in late winter/early spring for summer placements; positions are competitive

name: Youth Volunteer Corps (YVC)
summary: A national network of structured, team-based service-learning programs for youth ages 11–18 that builds life and work skills through supervised volunteer projects year-round.
subject: Mixed
description: YVC affiliates across the U.S. and Canada run the same structured program model, engaging youth in supervised, diverse team-based projects in partnership with nonprofits, YMCAs, United Ways, Boys & Girls Clubs, and more. Projects span a wide range of service areas and occur throughout the school year and summer. The program emphasizes teamwork, communication, problem-solving, and developing a lifelong ethic of service. A 2025 Impact Report confirms the program is actively running.
eligibility: Ages 11–18; must have a local YVC affiliate in their community (27+ programs across U.S. and Canada)
cost: Free to participants
deadline: Rolling enrollment; contact local YVC affiliate to participate

name: Amnesty International USA – Youth Leadership in Activism (YLA)
summary: A structured national volunteer leadership program for high school and college youth with Amnesty groups, spanning roles as Peer Trainers, Student Activist Coordinators, and Social Media Managers.
subject: Law
description: YLA encompasses four distinct member leader roles through which youth provide peer-to-peer coaching, training, and resource-sharing to AIUSA's 600+ student groups across the country. Leaders build skills in organizing, advocacy, communications, and coalition-building while driving human rights campaigns. A complementary tier, the Youth Collective (YoCo), serves ages 15–24 as a national strategy body. Applications typically open annually; the 2025–2026 cohort's applications are confirmed closed, indicating a recurring annual cycle.
eligibility: High school students with at least one year of Amnesty International experience recommended; ages 15–24 for YoCo tier; U.S.-based
cost: Volunteer role; unpaid but travel may be covered for select events (e.g., AGM)
deadline: YLA and YoCo applications open annually, typically in early spring; 2025–2026 applications are closed

name: American Junior Academy of Sciences (AJAS) Annual Conference
org: National Association of Academies of Science (NAAS)
summary: The only US honor society conference for high school students recognized for outstanding STEM research, held annually alongside the AAAS meeting. Delegates present research and are inducted as lifetime Fellows.
subject: STEM
description: AJAS meets each year in conjunction with the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) annual meeting. High school students are nominated as delegates by their state's Academy of Science and present original STEM research in poster sessions. The conference is not a competition but a celebration of student achievement, exposing delegates to plenary lectures, field trips, and small-group meetings with professional scientists. The 2026 conference was held in Phoenix, AZ in February 2026 alongside AAAS.
eligibility: Must be nominated by a state Academy of Science; US high school students
cost: Students typically responsible for travel, registration (~$1,200 estimated); scholarships available via NAAS-AJAS Scholarship Program
deadline: State-level nominations typically occur in fall; AJAS conference held in February alongside AAAS

name: AMIA Annual Symposium High School Scholars Program
summary: High school students who have conducted biomedical informatics research with a faculty mentor can present at AMIA's major annual professional symposium each November. Dedicated sessions, networking, and educational activities are included.
subject: Medicine
description: AMIA's Annual Symposium includes a dedicated High School Scholars Competition where selected students present research via oral or poster presentations to an audience of clinicians, scientists, and informaticists. Students must be enrolled in high school and have conducted research through a recognized biomedical informatics program or lab; individual submissions only. The 2026 symposium is scheduled for November in Dallas, Texas. Accepted students attend educational sessions and network alongside professionals in a rare high-school-level opportunity.
eligibility: Must be enrolled in high school; research must be conducted through a recognized biomedical informatics program or lab; individual submissions only
cost: Travel/registration costs apply; funding from research mentor may help but is not required for selection
deadline: Submission deadlines typically in spring/summer; check AMIA website for 2026 dates

name: International Young Researchers' Conference (IYRC)
summary: An interdisciplinary conference exclusively for high school student researchers to publish original work and present to an international audience. Held multiple times a year in-person and virtually, with the Summer 2026 edition planned at the University of Tokyo.
subject: Mixed
description: The IYRC, established in 2018, has hosted 12+ conferences attracting young researchers from 25+ countries with a 40–50% acceptance rate. Only high school students may submit research as first authors across any field. Accepted abstracts (750–1,500 words) are published in conference proceedings, and presenters must give live presentations. The Summer 2026 conference is tentatively planned in-person at the University of Tokyo, Japan, with a virtual option also available.
eligibility: High school students only; first author must be a high school student; research must be original and primarily conducted by student
cost: Registration fee required upon acceptance; financial aid available
deadline: Summer 2026 abstract submission deadline was May 31, 2026

name: NCSS Student Leadership & Research Conference
summary: An annual conference for grades 8–12 students to present original STEM research, participate in leadership sessions, and visit university research facilities. Held in Alpharetta, Georgia.
subject: STEM
description: The NCSS Student Leadership & Research Conference bridges rigorous student research with leadership development and entrepreneurship. Students present original research in structured sessions and engage in STEM leadership programming, conversations with active researchers, and visits to facilities like the Georgia Tech Research Institute. The 2026 conference was held July 16 at Fulton Science Academy in Alpharetta, GA. An NCSS participation certificate is awarded to each student.
eligibility: Students in grades 8–12 with original STEM research; open to NCSS member school students
cost: Hotel accommodations required at attendee expense; discounted group rate available
deadline: Registration for 2026 edition closed prior to July 16, 2026; check site for 2027 dates

name: RIT Student Research in Communication Conference
org: Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) School of Communication
summary: An annual regional conference held at RIT where graduate, undergraduate, and high school students present original research in communication and related disciplines. The 2026 edition was held April 2.
subject: Humanities
description: Hosted annually since 2004, this conference invites high school students alongside undergraduates and graduate students to submit research papers on any communication topic, including advertising, public relations, media studies, film, journalism, and AI in media. Works-in-progress and poster-format projects are also welcome. All research approaches—qualitative, quantitative, critical, and theoretical—are accepted. The event is open to the public for attendance.
eligibility: High school students with research in communication or related disciplines; open to all
cost: No submission or attendance fee noted; travel/hotel at attendee expense
deadline: Paper submission deadline typically in late winter/early spring; conference held in early April

name: Close Up Foundation Empowering Girls' Voices Student Summit
org: Close Up Foundation & International Coalition of Girls' Schools (ICGS)
summary: A Washington, D.C. summit for high school girls (grades 9–12) focused on civic leadership, policy priorities, and building empathy across perspectives. The 2026 edition ran February 3–6.
subject: Leadership
description: Organized in partnership with the International Coalition of Girls' Schools, the summit brings together high school girls in Washington, D.C. to share policy priorities, develop civic skills, and engage in facilitated deliberation on pressing national issues. The student summit runs parallel to a concurrent educator summit. Students build skills in inclusive dialogue, advocacy, and civic engagement. The program is open to all high school girls interested in civic action regardless of school affiliation.
eligibility: High school girls in grades 9–12 with interest in civic engagement; open to all schools
cost: Nonrefundable deposit of $1,550 required; final payment due ~December
deadline: Deposit due late November for the February summit; check site for upcoming cycles

name: MIT Beaver Works Summer Institute (BWSI)
org: MIT Lincoln Laboratory & MIT School of Engineering
summary: Rigorous, project-based 4-week summer STEM program for rising high school seniors covering robotics, AI, cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and more—hosted at MIT.
subject: Engineering
description: BWSI combines free online prerequisite coursework in the spring with a selective 4-week in-person or online summer session at MIT. Students work in teams on real engineering challenges in fields like autonomous vehicle racing, machine learning, radar, quantum computing, and cybersecurity. Courses are jointly offered by MIT Lincoln Laboratory and MIT's School of Engineering. Only students living and attending high school in the US are eligible for the summer in-person component.
eligibility: Must live and attend high school in the US; no higher than grade 11 (rising seniors); must complete online prerequisite course before applying to summer session
cost: Fully funded; free online prerequisite courses plus free summer program
deadline: Online course registration opens December; summer applications sent only to those who complete prerequisites (due ~April)

name: UMass Turing Summer Program
org: University of Massachusetts Amherst – Manning College of Information & Computer Sciences
summary: Free three-week day program at UMass Amherst for Western Massachusetts high school sophomores and juniors exploring CS applications in healthcare, energy, robotics, and AI.
subject: Computer Science
description: The program runs July 6–24, 2026, with daily classroom and lab sessions on programming, AI, robotics, cloud computing, 3D printing, cybersecurity, and data visualization using Python. No prior computing experience is required. The program is primarily designed for students who can commute daily to the UMass Amherst campus; housing is not provided. Non-local students are considered on a space-available basis.
eligibility: Primarily for rising 10th–11th graders at Western Massachusetts high schools; rising 9th graders and seniors may apply; no prior CS experience required
cost: No charge for local high school students; lunch provided
deadline: July 6–24, 2026; applications open until spots are filled

name: Harvard Society for AI – AI Bootcamp
org: Harvard Undergraduate Society for Artificial Intelligence (HUSAI)
summary: Intensive 5-day online AI/ML bootcamp for high school students, taught by Harvard graduate researchers, with four June 2026 cohorts and intro/advanced tracks.
subject: Computer Science
description: Developed and taught by Harvard grad-level researchers and undergraduates, this program covers machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, computer vision, reinforcement learning, and culminates in a mini-research project/hackathon. Two tracks are available: Intro (requires Python comfort and interest in math) and Advanced (requires AI/ML familiarity and mathematical rigor). The bootcamp runs online via Zoom in 2.75-hour daily sessions across four cohorts in June 2026.
eligibility: High school students; Python proficiency required; calculus experience preferred; exceptions for younger/older students considered case-by-case
cost: Paid; exact price not confirmed from search results
deadline: Rolling admissions until seats filled; June 2026 cohorts: June 1–5, 8–12, 15–19, 22–26

name: iD Tech Camps
summary: Week-long (and 2-week overnight) STEM camps held at 75+ universities nationwide, offering coding, AI, robotics, and game development courses for ages 7–17.
subject: Computer Science
description: iD Tech camps run as day camps or overnight Teen Academy sessions at prestigious university campuses including Stanford, MIT, Caltech, UCLA, and many others. Courses span Python/AI agents, machine learning, game development, robotics, and more, delivered in small groups by certified instructors. The program offers tracks from beginner to advanced levels. Teen Academy overnight sessions are 2 weeks for ages 13–18.
eligibility: Ages 7–17 (high school focus ages 13–17); beginner to advanced; no prerequisites for most courses
cost: Starting at ~$1,379 per week; payment plans available
deadline: Sessions available summer 2026; register early as sessions fill up

name: MIT Blueprint (HackMIT)
summary: Free weekend-long learnathon and hackathon for high school students of all skill levels, held in-person at MIT each spring.
subject: Computer Science
description: Blueprint 2026 took place February 28 – March 1 at MIT's campus. Participants learn coding from MIT students through workshops in programming fundamentals, web development, game development, and hardware, then form teams to build and demo a CS project to judges for prizes. No prior coding experience is required. The event is entirely free and open to all high school students.
eligibility: Any high school student; all skill levels welcome; must attend in person
cost: Free to attend; travel/housing not provided
deadline: Blueprint 2026 held Feb 28–Mar 1, 2026; applications closed Feb 1, 2026; watch for 2027 dates

name: HackAmerica
summary: America's largest online hackathon exclusively for US high school students ages 13–19, with no required theme and an open-ended project format.
subject: Computer Science
description: HackAmerica 2026 ran April 11 – May 23, 2026 entirely online via Devpost. Students ages 13–19 can build any type of project—social impact apps, games, personal tools—using any tech stack they choose. It is beginner-friendly with design and social good tracks. The competition is limited to US high school students only.
eligibility: US high school students only; ages 13–19; beginner-friendly
cost: Free to enter
deadline: 2026 edition ran Apr 11 – May 23, 2026; check Devpost for future editions

name: Hack Club – High School Hackathons Directory
summary: Curated, staff-maintained directory of 800+ in-person and online high school hackathons worldwide, with 116 events across 30 US states and 26 countries in 2026.
subject: Computer Science
description: Hack Club maintains a living list of high school hackathons spanning year-round events globally. Students can filter by location (US states, international), date, and format. Events range from large flagship hackathons to small local one-day events. Hack Club also runs its own flagship annual in-person hackathon for high schoolers.
eligibility: High school students; eligibility varies by individual hackathon
cost: Most listed hackathons are free to enter; individual events vary
deadline: Year-round events; check site for current and upcoming hackathons

name: NGN Hacks 2026
summary: Global online hackathon for high school students in grades 9–12, open to beginners and experienced coders, focused on building real-world tech solutions.
subject: Computer Science
description: NGN Hacks 2026 ran August 7–9, 2026 entirely online. Students worldwide in grades 9–12 can build solo or in teams across categories like AI, education, sustainability, health, accessibility, cybersecurity, and productivity. No expert coding skills are required; the goal is learning, collaboration, and portfolio-building. Judges included engineers from companies like Lyft, Motorola, and Lucid Motors.
eligibility: High school students grades 9–12 worldwide; beginners welcome
cost: Free to enter
deadline: 2026 edition ran August 7–9, 2026; watch Devpost for future editions

name: hackTAMS
org: Texas Academy of Mathematics and Science (TAMS)
summary: Annual high school hackathon organized by TAMS students at UNT, open to Texas high schoolers ages 13–19, with workshops, guest speakers, and open-ended coding projects.
subject: Computer Science
description: hackTAMS 2026 ran February 28 – March 1, 2026. High school students design, build, and present a software or hardware project within the hackathon window. The event is beginner-friendly and includes workshops, guest speakers, and networking opportunities. Only US high school students (ages 13–19) are eligible; professional organizations are excluded.
eligibility: US high school students ages 13–19; no professionals; beginner-friendly
cost: Free to enter
deadline: 2026 edition: Feb 28–Mar 1, 2026; watch for 2027 announcement

name: University of Iowa AI Youth Camp
summary: Free two-week online AI camp for high school students in grades 9–11, covering machine learning, reinforcement learning, and engineering ethics using real NSF/NASA datasets.
subject: Computer Science
description: The fourth annual AI Youth Camp runs June 8–19, 2026 on Zoom, directed by University of Iowa professors. Topics include machine learning, reinforcement learning, and engineering ethics, with open-source datasets from NSF, the Office of Naval Research, and NASA. Basic coding skills are required and registration is limited to 30 participants.
eligibility: High school students grades 9–11; basic coding skills required; limited to 30 participants
cost: Free
deadline: June 8–19, 2026; apply early as spots are very limited

name: Purdue University Northwest High School Summer Engineering Camp
org: Purdue University Northwest – College of Engineering and Sciences
summary: Free one-week in-person mechanical and civil engineering camp for students ages 14–17 at PNW's Hammond Campus, including 3D printing, renewable energy, VR, and EV go-carts.
subject: Engineering
description: The camp runs July 6–10, 2026 at Purdue University Northwest's Hammond, Indiana campus. Students participate in interactive lab and classroom activities covering mechanical and civil engineering topics including 3D printing, renewable energy, bridge/road design, virtual reality, and electric cars. Participants also build a balsa wood bridge, cardboard wind tunnel, and EV go-cart. The camp is completely free.
eligibility: Students ages 14–17
cost: Free
deadline: July 6–10, 2026; register early

name: University of Arizona Summer Engineering Academy (SEA)
org: University of Arizona College of Engineering
summary: Multi-week on-campus engineering camp for high school students at the University of Arizona, covering 18 engineering disciplines through hands-on projects and lab experiences.
subject: Engineering
description: SEA 2026 offers high school students multiple weeks of camp on the UA campus with activities across the college's 18 engineering disciplines. No prior engineering experience is required. Students engage in engineering projects, presentations, and real-life lab experiences. Registration opened March 2, 2026, on a first-come, first-served basis through June 30, 2026.
eligibility: High school students; no prior engineering experience required; all educational backgrounds welcome
cost: Paid; financial aid available
deadline: Registration open March 2 – June 30, 2026, or until full; first-come, first-served
